written.q: Give three reasons for virtualizing servers. (3 marks)
written.a: Effective resource usage (CPU, RAM, disk allocated where needed); ease of management (unused VMs kept off, easier provisioning, maintenance, HA and DR); security (applications isolated on separate VMs that do not risk each other, even for mutually untrusting users).

written.q: Compare full virtualization, para-virtualization and hardware-assisted virtualization. (9)
written.a: Full virtualization uses binary translation: the hypervisor rewrites sensitive guest kernel instructions on the fly, so unmodified OSes run (VMware ESXi, Hyper-V); simple setup but translation costs performance. Para-virtualization modifies the guest kernel to call the hypervisor through hypercalls instead of privileged instructions; best performance but needs a modified OS (Xen on traditional hardware, Oracle VM Server). Hardware-assisted virtualization uses CPU extensions (Intel VT-x, AMD-V) so sensitive instructions trap to the hypervisor in hardware and the guest can execute certain instructions directly; unmodified guests, simpler hypervisor code and higher performance, but needs CPU support enabled in the BIOS.

written.q: Explain the three generations of hardware-assisted virtualization. (6)
written.a: CPU: Intel VT-x / AMD-V (2006) add a guest mode; need DEP (Intel XD, AMD NX) enabled in BIOS and a power cycle. MMU: Intel EPT / AMD RVI (NPT) do two-level address translation in hardware, removing shadow page tables (up to 48%/42% gains on MMU-heavy benchmarks). I/O: Intel VT-d / AMD-Vi IOMMU remaps DMA and interrupts so VMs can access devices such as NICs directly (VMware VMDirectPath I/O), lowering CPU cost.

Xen: Type 1 hypervisor running multiple OSes, supporting para-virtualization and hardware virtualization. KVM: Type 1 hypervisor built into the Linux kernel, turning Linux into a bare-metal hypervisor using hardware assistance. LXC: not a hypervisor but OS-level virtualization, running isolated Linux containers that share the host kernel.

written.q: Compare ESXi with vSphere and describe vCenter Server. (5)
written.a: ESXi is the free, production-class bare-metal hypervisor for partitioning a single server with advanced resource management. vSphere is the suite that pools many ESXi hosts into resources with centralized management, automation and availability; all editions include ESXi. vCenter Server is the central administration point that manages multiple ESXi hosts and directs actions on VMs and hosts, with a database for configuration and the vSphere Client/Web Access as interfaces.

written.q: What is vMotion? Describe its steps. (9)
written.a: vMotion is live migration of a running VM between hosts without downtime; shared VMFS storage lets both hosts access the VM's files, so memory and execution state are sent over a fast network and the VM keeps its network identity. Steps: request ESX1 → ESX2; vCenter checks the VM is stable and ESX2 is compatible; VM registered on ESX2; memory, registers and network state copied while changes are tracked in a memory bitmap on ESX1; VM quiesced on ESX1 and the bitmap copied; VM started on ESX2 and requests redirected; final memory copy; VM unregistered from ESX1; VM resumes on ESX2.

written.q: Distinguish vMotion and Storage vMotion. Outline Storage vMotion. (6)
written.a: vMotion moves a running VM to another host while its storage stays put; Storage vMotion keeps the VM on the same host but moves its disk files to another datastore. Storage vMotion: create the target directory and copy config files; self-vMotion to the target directory; snapshot the source disks; copy the disks; consolidate the snapshot into the target disks; delete the source files.

written.q: Explain DRS, VMware HA and Site Recovery Manager. (6)
written.a: DRS (Distributed Resource Scheduler) automatically balances workloads across hosts within set limits and guarantees, using vMotion, so resource assignment need not be predicted. VMware HA protects servers and applications against component and whole-host failure by restarting affected VMs on other hosts. SRM automates failover from the production site to a disaster-recovery site and allows non-disruptive DR testing.

written.q: How does a vSwitch differ from a physical switch? (6)
written.a: Like a physical switch, it forwards by MAC address and supports VLANs (802.1Q tagging) and EtherChannels. Unlike one, it does not need to learn MAC addresses (it knows each connected vNIC's MAC), does not take part in spanning tree, and has no trunks between vSwitches, so loops are impossible without a bridging VM. VM-to-VM traffic on the same vSwitch stays local; unknown destinations go out through the vmnic uplink.

written.q: What problems does Cisco Nexus 1000V/VN-Link solve? (4)
written.a: When vMotion moves VMs across physical ports, network and security policy must follow the VM; locally switched VM-to-VM traffic could not be seen or policed; traffic from many VMs on one link could not be distinguished. Nexus 1000V is a distributed virtual switch whose VN-Link extends the network to each VM, with policy-based connectivity that moves with the VM and visibility during vMotion.

written.q: In Lab 01, explain each part of the nmcli command that sets a static IP and how you verify it. (6)
written.a: nmcli connection modify ens160 edits the ens160 connection; ipv4.addresses 192.168.8.X/24 sets the host address with a 255.255.255.0 mask; ipv4.gateway 192.168.8.1 sets the default router; ipv4.dns "8.8.8.8 1.1.1.1" sets DNS servers; ipv4.method manual switches from DHCP to static. Restart with nmcli connection down/up ens160. Verify with ip addr (address), ip route (default via 192.168.8.1), ping 8.8.8.8 (Internet by IP) and ping www.google.com (DNS working).
